exercises.title: Scaling a Recipe
exercises.prompt:
A home cook found a recipe written for one batch size but needs a different amount today.

Write `scale_recipe(amounts, factor)` that takes a list of ingredient amounts in grams and a scaling `factor`, and returns a NEW list where each amount is multiplied by `factor` and rounded to 1 decimal place. The original list of amounts must not be changed by your function.

Example: `scale_recipe([100, 50, 25], 2.0)` returns `[200.0, 100.0, 50.0]`.
exercises.referenceSolution:
def scale_recipe(amounts, factor):
    return [round(a * factor, 1) for a in amounts]

exercises.title: Weekend Activity Groups
exercises.prompt:
A community center collects sign-up slips for its Saturday activities. Each slip lists a person's name and the activity they picked, in the order the slips came in.

Write `group_signups(entries)` that takes a list of `[name, activity]` pairs and returns a dictionary mapping each activity to the list of names who picked it, in the order they signed up. Activities must appear in the dictionary in the order they were first chosen.

Example: `group_signups([["Mona", "yoga"], ["Sam", "chess"], ["Lina", "yoga"]])` returns `{"yoga": ["Mona", "Lina"], "chess": ["Sam"]}`.

exercises.title: Guest List Overlap
exercises.prompt:
Alia and Ben are each drafting a guest list for a joint party, and a few names got written down more than once by mistake.

Write `guest_summary(list_a, list_b)` that takes two lists of guest names and returns a list of three lists: names that appear on both lists, names that appear only on `list_a`, and names that appear only on `list_b`. Each of the three lists must be sorted alphabetically, and a name repeated within one list should only count once.

Example: `guest_summary(["Sam", "Lee", "Sam"], ["Lee", "Omar"])` returns `[["Lee"], ["Sam"], ["Omar"]]`.
exercises.referenceSolution:
def guest_summary(list_a, list_b):
    set_a = set(list_a)
    set_b = set(list_b)
    both = sorted(set_a & set_b)
    only_a = sorted(set_a - set_b)
    only_b = sorted(set_b - set_a)
    return [both, only_a, only_b]

exercises.title: Claiming Items From a List
exercises.prompt:
Two roommates keep one shared shopping list on the fridge. When someone heads to the store, they claim a few items to buy without erasing anyone else's view of the list.

Write `claim_items(shared_list, items_to_claim)`. Build a new list that starts as a copy of `shared_list` and removes the FIRST matching occurrence of each name in `items_to_claim` (skip a name that is not present, and process names in the order given). Return a list with two elements: the new list of remaining items, followed by `shared_list` itself, which must still hold every original item in its original order.

Example: `claim_items(["milk", "eggs", "bread", "eggs"], ["eggs"])` returns `[["milk", "bread", "eggs"], ["milk", "eggs", "bread", "eggs"]]`.

exercises.title: Character Sheet Mix-Up
exercises.prompt:
A small role-playing game stores each player's stats in a dictionary. Two friends are looking at what they believe are two separate character sheets before a session.

What does this program print? Write the exact output, one line per `print` call.

Example: if `a = {"x": 1}` and `b = a`, changing `b["x"]` also changes what `a` shows, because `b` is just another name for the same dictionary; `a.copy()` instead makes a separate dictionary that can change independently.

```python
p1 = {"name": "Rex", "level": 1}
p2 = p1
p2["level"] = 2
p3 = p1.copy()
p3["level"] = 3
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(p3)
```
exercises.referenceSolution:
p1 = {"name": "Rex", "level": 1}
p2 = p1
p2["level"] = 2
p3 = p1.copy()
p3["level"] = 3
print(p1)
print(p2)
print(p3)

exercises.title: Locate a crate on the dock
exercises.prompt:
A dock manager scans shipping crates as they come off the truck and needs to check whether a specific crate has already been logged, and where.

Write `find_crate(codes, target)` that looks through the list of crate codes in order and returns the position of the first crate whose code equals `target`. If the crate is not in the list, return `-1`.

Example: `find_crate(["A12", "B77", "C03"], "C03")` returns `2`. `find_crate(["A12", "B77"], "Z99")` returns `-1`.

exercises.title: First alarm trigger
exercises.prompt:
A home security panel logs one motion-sensor reading per minute, each a number from `0` (no motion) upward. The app wants to know which minute first crossed the sensitivity threshold.

Write `first_alarm(readings, threshold)` that returns the 1-based position of the first reading strictly greater than `threshold`. If no reading crosses the threshold, return `-1`.

Example: `first_alarm([0, 2, 5, 1], 4)` returns `3` (the third reading, 5, is the first above 4). `first_alarm([1, 1, 1], 9)` returns `-1`.

tests.name: value equal to threshold never triggers

exercises.title: Sort racers by finish time
exercises.prompt:
A trail race records each runner's bib number and finish time in the order they crossed the line, but organizers want the official ranking ordered fastest to slowest.

Write `rank_by_time(bibs, times)` that returns a new list of bib numbers ordered from smallest to largest `times` value. Build the ranking by repeatedly scanning the list and swapping any adjacent pair that is out of order, continuing until no swap is needed. `bibs[i]` and `times[i]` always describe the same runner, and if two runners tie exactly, keep the one that appeared first in `bibs` ahead of the other.

Example: `rank_by_time([101, 102, 103], [12.4, 9.9, 11.0])` returns `[102, 103, 101]`.

exercises.title: Trim silence from a clip
exercises.prompt:
An audio app records a volume level for every sampled moment in a short clip, where `0` means silence. Before saving, it trims away any silence at the very start and the very end, but keeps quiet gaps that occur in the middle of the sound.

Write `trim_silence(levels)` that returns a new list with the leading and trailing zeros removed. If every sample is `0`, or the list is empty, return an empty list.

Example: `trim_silence([0, 0, 3, 0, 5, 0, 0])` returns `[3, 0, 5]`. `trim_silence([2, 4])` returns `[2, 4]`.

exercises.title: Find the price cutoff
exercises.prompt:
A box office keeps every sold ticket price in one list, already sorted from cheapest to priciest, and duplicate prices are common. Staff want to know where a new price would land if it were inserted to keep the list sorted, so they can quote how many tickets already cost less than it.

Write `lower_bound(prices, target)` that returns the smallest position `i` for which `prices[i] >= target`. If every price is below `target`, return `len(prices)`. The list can be long, so narrow the range you check instead of comparing against every price from the start.

Example: `lower_bound([10, 10, 20, 30, 30, 30, 50], 30)` returns `3`. `lower_bound([5, 8, 12], 20)` returns `3`.

tests.name: target matches middle of a run

exercises.title: Rank players on a leaderboard
exercises.prompt:
A retro arcade cabinet logs today's runs as a list of dictionaries, each with `name`, `score`, and `attempts` (how many tries it took to reach that score). The high-score screen should list players from best to worst using Python's sorting tools rather than a hand-written comparison loop.

Write `leaderboard(players)` that returns a list of names ordered by: highest `score` first; when scores tie, fewer `attempts` first; when that also ties, `name` in alphabetical order.

Example: `leaderboard([{"name": "Ana", "score": 50, "attempts": 3}, {"name": "Bo", "score": 50, "attempts": 1}, {"name": "Cy", "score": 80, "attempts": 5}])` returns `["Cy", "Bo", "Ana"]`.

exercises.title: Fuel stop summary
exercises.prompt:
A road trip app records every fuel stop as a pair of numbers: how many liters were pumped and the price paid per liter. Some stations charge a premium price above `1.50` per liter.

Write `trip_summary(stops)` where `stops` is a list of `(liters, price_per_liter)` pairs. For each stop, work out its cost (liters times price, rounded to 2 decimals) and whether it counts as premium (price strictly greater than `1.50`). Combine those results into one summary: return a tuple `(total_cost, premium_count)`, where `total_cost` is the rounded sum of every stop's cost and `premium_count` is how many stops were premium. A trip with no stops returns `(0, 0)`.

A station charging exactly `1.50` does not count as premium.

Example: `trip_summary([(10, 1.2), (5, 1.6)])` returns `(20.0, 1)`.

exercises.title: Weekly rainfall recap
exercises.prompt:
A small weather station logs each day's rainfall in millimetres for a week, alongside the day's name.

Write `rainfall_summary(readings)` where `readings` is a list of `(day_name, rainfall_mm)` pairs. Return a tuple `(total_mm, wettest_day)`: the total rainfall across every entry, and the name of the day with the single highest reading. When two or more days share the highest reading, use whichever one appears first in the list. An empty list of readings returns `(0, None)`.

Example: `rainfall_summary([("Mon", 5.0), ("Tue", 12.5), ("Wed", 0.0)])` returns `(17.5, "Tue")`.

exercises.title: Low stock finder
exercises.prompt:
A small warehouse tracks each item's current quantity and its reorder level: the quantity at or below which it must be reordered.

Write `needs_restock(inventory)` where `inventory` is a list of `(item_name, quantity, reorder_level)` triples. Return a list of the item names whose quantity is strictly less than their reorder level, in the same order as the input. An item exactly at its reorder level does not need restocking yet. An empty inventory returns an empty list.

Example: `needs_restock([("bolts", 5, 10), ("nails", 20, 15), ("screws", 8, 8)])` returns `["bolts"]`.

exercises.title: Trail distance converter
exercises.prompt:
A hiking app stores each trail's length in miles and wants to show hikers the metric equivalent instead.

Write `to_kilometers(trails)` where `trails` is a list of `(trail_name, miles)` pairs. Return a new list of `(trail_name, kilometers)` pairs, in the same order, where each length is converted using `1 mile = 1.60934 km` and rounded to 1 decimal place. An empty list returns an empty list.

Example: `to_kilometers([("Ridge Loop", 5), ("River Path", 2)])` returns `[("Ridge Loop", 8.0), ("River Path", 3.2)]`.
exercises.referenceSolution:
def to_kilometers(trails):
    return [(name, round(miles * 1.60934, 1)) for name, miles in trails]

exercises.title: Game night picker
exercises.prompt:
A group picks the next board game to play by shouting out votes. The host keeps a short list of games available tonight, in the order she'd prefer to break ties.

Write `pick_next_game(games, votes)` where `games` is a list of the available game names and `votes` is a list of shouted-out names (some might not be on the list at all, and should be ignored). Return a tuple `(chosen_game, vote_count)` for the game with the most valid votes. If two or more games tie for the most votes, pick whichever one appears earliest in `games`. If nobody voted, or every vote was invalid, return the first game in `games` with a count of `0`.

Example: `pick_next_game(["Chess", "Uno", "Catan"], ["Uno", "Uno", "Chess", "Catan"])` returns `("Uno", 2)`.

exercises.title: Cash register line parser
exercises.prompt:
A cash register saves each sale as one line of plain text in the form `item,quantity,unit_price`. Lines sometimes end with a trailing newline character and sometimes have extra spaces around the commas.

Write `parse_sale_line(line)` that splits the line into its three fields, strips whitespace (including any trailing newline) from each one, converts the quantity to an `int` and the unit price to a `float`, and returns them as a list `[item, quantity, unit_price]`.

Example: `parse_sale_line("Apples, 3 , 0.50\n")` returns `["Apples", 3, 0.5]`.
exercises.referenceSolution:
def parse_sale_line(line):
    parts = line.strip().split(',')
    item = parts[0].strip()
    quantity = int(parts[1].strip())
    unit_price = float(parts[2].strip())
    return [item, quantity, unit_price]

exercises.title: Attendance row cleanup
exercises.prompt:
A weekly attendance sheet is exported to a plain text file, one row per student split into three fields: name, status, and minutes late. Some cells come out blank, and a few minutes-late values get corrupted during export.

Write `clean_attendance_row(fields)` where `fields` is `[name, status, minutes_late]` (all strings). Return `None` when `name` is blank. Otherwise strip whitespace from every field, default a blank `status` to `"present"`, and turn `minutes_late` into an `int` that defaults to `0` whenever it is blank, not a whole number, or negative.

Example: `clean_attendance_row(["Sara", "late", "5"])` returns `["Sara", "late", 5]`. `clean_attendance_row(["", "present", "0"])` returns `None`.

exercises.title: Coffee order revenue totals
exercises.prompt:
A coffee shop exports its order log as rows with a drink name, size, and price, but a few price cells come back blank whenever the register's scanner missed a scan.

Write `total_revenue_by_drink(records)` where `records` is a list of dicts with keys `"drink"`, `"size"`, and `"price"` (all strings, as they would be straight out of a CSV reader). Sum the price for each drink, skipping any record whose price is blank instead of crashing. Leave out any drink whose every price was blank. Return a list of `[drink, total]` pairs sorted alphabetically by drink name, with each total rounded to 2 decimals.

Example: two Latte orders priced `"4.50"` and `"5.00"` plus one Tea order priced `"2.00"` return `[["Latte", 9.5], ["Tea", 2.0]]`.

tests.name: one blank price still counts the drink
